title: Spatial symmetry invariance of three-dimensional Navier-Stokes turbulence
authors: Shijun Liao
abstract: Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) of the deterministic Navier-Stokes (NS) equations is widely used to provide benchmark solutions of turbulent flow, but its accuracy and reliability have not been rigorously inspected from a mathematical viewpoint. Here we prove a spatial symmetry invariance theorem (SSIT) of three-dimensional NS equations whereby an exact solution of deterministic NS equations under periodic boundary conditions maintains the same spatial symmetry as its symmetric initial flow, forever. SSIT provides an absolute benchmark test for computational fluid dynamics (CFD). It is shown herein that traditional DNS of NS turbulence quickly violates SSIT, revealing that the spatiotemporal trajectory of NS turbulence predicted by DNS soon becomes badly polluted by numerical noise. Importantly, it is found that even the statistical results of DNS might be unstable, i.e., exhibit sensitivity dependence on the initial flow conditions. In other words, the loss of spatial symmetry in traditional DNS of NS turbulence is not a physical instability but instead a numerical artifact caused by the chaotic nature of the flow. Using the SSIT, it is straightforward to deduce several key properties of NS turbulence, including `ultra-chaos', the so-called `noise-expansion cascade', `permanent memory of symmetric initial flow conditions', and so on. Note that permanent memory of symmetric initial flow conditions suggests that NS turbulence governed by deterministic NS equations subject to symmetric initial flow should have no `mixing', corresponding to non-ergodicity, although ergodicity is one of the most fundamental assumptions of turbulence theory.

infographic.key_insight: The paper presents a spatial symmetry invariance theorem stating that exact three-dimensional Navier–Stokes solutions with periodic boundaries preserve symmetric initial-flow structure, providing a benchmark for numerical simulations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Monitoring symmetry preservation could help CFD practitioners detect numerical contamination in turbulent-flow simulations.
method: Derive a spatial symmetry invariance theorem for deterministic Navier–Stokes equations.
Test traditional DNS against symmetry preservation.
Examine implications for statistical sensitivity and memory of initial conditions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports rapid symmetry violations in traditional DNS and possible sensitivity of computed statistics to initial conditions, but provides no quantitative errors or simulation settings.
infographic.watch_item: Check the theorem’s solution-existence and uniqueness assumptions and the numerical convergence evidence before generalizing its claims about turbulence statistics or non-ergodicity.
infographic.paper_title: Spatial symmetry invariance of three-dimensional Navier-Stokes turbulence

title: Generative AI in Turbulence: Foundations, Applications, Validations and Benchmarks
authors: Luca Biferale, Michele Buzzicotti
abstract: Generative AI offers new approaches to turbulence problems in which incomplete observations or unresolved d.o.f. admit multiple physically plausible solutions. Potential applications include stochastic closures, super-resolution, data assimilation, uncertainty quantification, and the generation of Eulerian and Lagrangian flow ensembles. However, turbulence is not a conventional image-generation problem. Its multiscale dynamics, intermittency, extreme events, rough velocity fields and intrinsically stochastic transport make visual realism, pointwise error, and low-order spectral agreement insufficient measures of physical fidelity. We examine where generative AI provide novel capabilities with emphasis on diffusion models, score-based methods, and related probability-transport formulations. We discuss their use in unconditional generation, probabilistic reconstruction, reduced-order modeling, temporal evolution, and mesh-free representations. We argue that validation must address turbulence properties: energy transfer, structure functions, anomalous scaling, pdf tails, coherent structures, conservation laws, temporal consistency, ensemble diversity and generalization. Finally, we discuss potential limitations in validation, baseline, data availability and reproducibility, and the need for a benchmark ecosystem combining open data, standardized challenges, hidden tests, physics-aware metrics, and documented failures. This paper serves as a bridge between two communities. For AI practitioners, we provide a fair and accessible introduction to turbulence, essential for appreciating the challenges posed by the field and for assessing the physical relevance of generative models. For turbulent practitioners, we provide an introduction to the key technological aspects of Generative AI, clarifying what these tools actually do, and where their potential and current limitations lie.

infographic.key_insight: Generative AI can produce multiple plausible turbulent flows from incomplete information, but physical fidelity requires validation beyond visual realism and low-order statistics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Potential uses include stochastic closures, flow super-resolution, data assimilation, and uncertainty quantification for under-resolved turbulence.
method: Reviews diffusion, score-based, and related probability-transport models.
Examines flow generation, probabilistic reconstruction, reduced-order modeling, and temporal evolution.
Proposes physics-aware validation and a reproducible benchmark ecosystem.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports no quantitative model results; it advocates evaluation of energy transfer, intermittency, conservation, temporal consistency, ensemble diversity, and generalization.
infographic.watch_item: Limited data, inadequate baselines, and incomplete validation can conceal physically incorrect predictions.
infographic.paper_title: Generative AI in Turbulence: Foundations, Applications, Validations and Benchmarks

title: Free-vortex-wake dynamics of airborne wind energy kites in crosswind flight
authors: Yinong Tian, Shan Wang
abstract: The wake of an airborne wind energy kite is shaped by its crosswind path and, for on-board generation, by the slipstreams of its rotors, and in farms it reaches downstream units. It is computed here by a vortex step method with a time-marching free vortex wake, implemented by the authors in their open-source code OpenFAWE with a lumped-mass tether, actuator-disc rotors releasing vortex rings and several kites. It reproduces an independent vortex step code to 10^-9 on the rigid-wing Makani M600 and within 0.3% in lift and 0.9% in drag on the TU Delft V3 leading-edge inflatable kite, matching its Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes lift within 3.1%. For fixed kites the lift deficit of a finite wake is the far field of its starting vortex, which fixes the wake length before a run, and the vortex core must stay below the narrowest panel width. With these settings the helical tip-vortex pair of the M600 on its loop lowers its lift by about 0.5% from 5 to 13 m/s. Free rotor rings do not converge with the time step, whereas an undeformed slipstream tube converges once its rings are refined at the wing and raises the lift by 1.9%. A slipstream deflected by the wing lowers it by 3.5%, so the treatment near the wing sets the sign of the rotor effect. A second unit one loop diameter downstream loses 0.5% of its lift and 2.2% of its aerodynamic power, with or without rotors.

infographic.key_insight: Rotor-slipstream modeling near the wing can reverse the predicted lift effect, outweighing the roughly 0.5% lift reduction from the kite’s helical wake.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Reliable wake predictions can inform airborne wind energy rotor integration and farm spacing, where a downstream kite lost 2.2% of aerodynamic power in the studied configuration.
method: Vortex step aerodynamics coupled to a time-marching free vortex wake in OpenFAWE.
Lumped-mass tether and actuator-disc rotors releasing vortex rings.
Single- and two-kite simulations comparing wake and slipstream treatments.
infographic.evidence_signal: Validation reproduced an independent vortex step code to 10^-9 for the M600 and within 0.3% in lift and 0.9% in drag for the V3 kite; V3 lift agreed with Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes results within 3.1%.
infographic.watch_item: Free rotor rings did not converge with time-step refinement, and alternative slipstream treatments predicted opposite lift changes (+1.9% versus −3.5%).
infographic.paper_title: Free-vortex-wake dynamics of airborne wind energy kites in crosswind flight

title: Toward fully stabilized flow control using deep reinforcement learning
authors: Wang Jia, Hang Xu
abstract: This study enhances the performance of flow control across various synthetic jet configurations by improving deep reinforcement learning techniques. The training results based on the foundational deep reinforcement learning framework indicate that as the Reynolds number increases, the effectiveness of synthetic jet control becomes increasingly sensitive to the position of the jet. When synthetic jets are positioned near the flow separation region, the control strategy consistently exhibits excellent performance. However, when synthetic jets are located farther from the separation region, the flow control performance diminishes, and the consumption of external energy increases. By enhancing dynamic state features and reshaping the reward function, we significantly improve control performance across various Reynolds numbers and synthetic jet positions. With the optimized framework, we achieve significant drag reduction effects ranging from 8% to 34% within the Reynolds number range of 100 to 400. The flow control strategy is capable of simultaneously achieving multiple control objectives, including reducing drag, suppressing lift, eliminating vortex shedding, and decreasing energy consumption. These findings highlight the potential of optimizing deep reinforcement learning frameworks to achieve more adaptive flow control strategies for various flow scenarios.

infographic.key_insight: Enhancing dynamic state features and reshaping rewards makes deep reinforcement learning flow control more effective across synthetic jet positions and Reynolds numbers.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Adaptive synthetic jet control can reduce drag, suppress lift and vortex shedding, and lower actuation energy consumption.
method: Train deep reinforcement learning controllers for multiple synthetic jet positions.
Enhance dynamic state features and reshape the reward function.
Evaluate control across Reynolds numbers from 100 to 400.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 8%–34% drag reduction with the optimized framework over Reynolds numbers of 100–400, alongside improvements in other control objectives.
infographic.watch_item: Performance beyond Reynolds numbers of 100–400 and transfer to physical flow-control hardware are not established by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Toward fully stabilized flow control using deep reinforcement learning

title: From Stochastic Transport Models to High-Dimensional Bayesian Inference
authors: Dan Crisan, Oana Lang
abstract: The Stochastic Transport in Upper Ocean Dynamics project introduced a new paradigm for representing uncertainty in geophysical fluid dynamics through stochastic transport models calibrated from data. This paper provides a synthesis of the principal theoretical and data assimilation developments achieved as part of the project. The central theme of the paper is the transformation of stochastic transport models from a modelling paradigm into a mathematically rigorous framework equipped with analytical, variational, calibration and Bayesian data assimilation methodologies suitable for geophysical fluid dynamics. We describe the development of the theory of stochastic transport equations, including well-posedness, regularity and approximation results, together with their geometric foundations based on stochastic variational principles, rough paths and fractional transport models. We further review methodologies for calibrating stochastic transport structures from observational and high-resolution simulation data, ranging from reduced-order stochastic models to modern generative approaches. Finally, we discuss Bayesian inference and high-dimensional data assimilation techniques developed for stochastic transport models, including particle filter methodologies and machine learning uncertainty quantification. Taken together, these developments establish a coherent framework linking stochastic transport modelling, rigorous analysis, calibration and Bayesian inference, thereby providing a foundation for uncertainty quantification and forecasting in geophysical fluid dynamics.

infographic.key_insight: Stochastic transport connects uncertainty modelling in geophysical fluids with rigorous analysis, data-driven calibration and high-dimensional Bayesian inference.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework provides a foundation for uncertainty-aware ocean forecasting and assimilation of observations into fluid models.
method: Establish well-posedness, regularity and approximation results using stochastic variational principles and rough-path methods.
Calibrate stochastic transport structures from observations and high-resolution simulations using reduced-order and generative models.
Develop Bayesian data assimilation through particle filters and machine-learning uncertainty quantification.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract synthesizes theoretical and methodological developments but reports no datasets, quantitative benchmarks or forecast improvements.
infographic.watch_item: Practical deployment requires validation of calibration quality and computational scalability in high-dimensional geophysical systems.
infographic.paper_title: From Stochastic Transport Models to High-Dimensional Bayesian Inference

title: Submerged Immiscible Oil Jet: Breakup Dynamics and Droplet Size Modelling
authors: Lokendra Mohan Sharma, Aditya K. Aiyer, Harish N. Dixit, Lakshmana Dora Chandrala
abstract: Immiscible liquid-liquid jets occur in numerous industrial and environmental settings, including oil spill response and liquid-liquid extraction, yet the coupled evolution of turbulence, interfacial instability, and droplet size distribution across transitional to turbulent regimes remains poorly understood. We present a combined experimental and theoretical investigation of a silicone oil jet injected into refractive-index-matched sugar water, employing simultaneous Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV) and Planar Laser-Induced Fluorescence (PLIF). Beyond the breakup region, mean velocity and Reynolds stress profiles exhibit self-similarity. Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) of the volume fraction reveals a systematic shift in the dominant instability mechanism with increasing Reynolds number: axisymmetric Rayleigh-Plateau modes govern breakup at low Reynolds numbers, sinuous and varicose modes coexist in the transitional regime, and Kelvin-Helmholtz-driven shear-layer breakup dominates at higher Reynolds numbers. Droplet sizes are extracted from PLIF images using a convolutional neural network-based segmentation approach. In the transitional regime, a bimodal droplet size distribution is observed, reflecting the coexistence of shear-induced breakup and Rayleigh-Plateau instability. As the Reynolds number increases and turbulent dissipation intensifies, the distribution evolves toward a single mode with smaller characteristic droplet sizes. To predict the droplet size distribution, existing population balance models are extended to include droplet coalescence. Incorporating coalescence substantially improves agreement with experimental measurements, particularly for larger droplets. These findings demonstrate that turbulent dissipation, interfacial instabilities, and droplet coalescence collectively govern the evolution of droplet size distribution in immiscible liquid-liquid jets.

infographic.key_insight: As Reynolds number increases, submerged oil-jet breakup shifts from Rayleigh–Plateau instability to shear-driven breakup, while droplet coalescence helps shape the resulting size distribution.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Accounting for both breakup and coalescence can improve droplet-size predictions for oil-spill response and liquid–liquid extraction.
method: Simultaneous PIV and PLIF measurements of silicone oil injected into refractive-index-matched sugar water.
POD identifies interfacial instability modes; CNN-based segmentation extracts droplet sizes.
Population balance models are extended to include droplet coalescence.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments show transitional bimodal droplet sizes evolving toward a smaller, single-mode distribution at higher Reynolds numbers, with coalescence improving model agreement especially for larger droplets.
infographic.watch_item: Transferability beyond the tested liquid pair requires validation; the abstract provides no quantitative prediction errors or segmentation accuracy.
infographic.paper_title: Submerged Immiscible Oil Jet: Breakup Dynamics and Droplet Size Modelling

title: A Systematic Assessment of Artificial Flame Thickening for Thermodiffusively Unstable Lean Hydrogen Flames in Homogeneous Isotropic Turbulence
authors: Max Schneider, Vinzenz Schuh, Felix Rong, Driss Kaddar, Andrew J. Aspden, Thomas L. Howarth
abstract: The Artificially Thickened Flame (ATF) approach is widely used to render premixed flames resolvable on coarse computational meshes, but thickening alters their interaction with turbulence. While considerable research has focused on the effects of thickening on turbulence-induced flame wrinkling, its influence on the mean local flame propagation speed in turbulent, thermodiffusively unstable hydrogen flames remains poorly understood. More than 200 flame-resolved simulations of premixed flames in homogeneous isotropic turbulence with detailed chemistry and transport are used to systematically isolate and quantify the effects of artificial thickening. Thickening the flame by a factor $F$ increases its effective flame-scale Karlovitz number according to $Ka_{\mathrm{f}}^F = Ka_{\mathrm{f}}\sqrt{F}$, while decreasing its effective Damköhler number according to $Da_{\mathrm{f}}^F = Da_{\mathrm{f}}/F$. In the regime considered here, the former enhances the mean local flame speed, whereas the latter reduces flame wrinkling, resulting in opposing effects on the flame consumption speed; hence, changes in both local flame propagation and flame area must be accounted for. Simulations matched with respect to $Ka_{\mathrm{f}}^F$ and $Da_{\mathrm{f}}^F$ collapse across different thickening factors $F$ until the thickened flame approaches the integral or geometric length scales of the configuration. Based on these scaling relations, a self-consistent efficiency correction is proposed to recover the unthickened flame consumption speed. Since the efficiency factor feeds back on the effective Karlovitz and Damköhler numbers, it must be determined implicitly.

infographic.key_insight: Artificial flame thickening increases effective flame-scale Karlovitz number and decreases Damköhler number, creating opposing effects on local propagation speed and flame wrinkling in lean hydrogen flames.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Accurate coarse-mesh hydrogen combustion predictions require corrections for both local flame propagation and flame area, not wrinkling alone.
method: Analyze over 200 flame-resolved simulations with detailed chemistry and transport in homogeneous isotropic turbulence.
Isolate thickening effects using Ka_f^F = Ka_f√F and Da_f^F = Da_f/F.
Propose an implicit, self-consistent efficiency correction to recover unthickened flame consumption speed.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations matched in effective Karlovitz and Damköhler numbers collapse across thickening factors until flame thickness approaches integral or geometric length scales.
infographic.watch_item: The proposed efficiency correction requires an implicit solution because it feeds back on effective flow–flame parameters; the reported collapse also has a scale-separation limit.
infographic.paper_title: A Systematic Assessment of Artificial Flame Thickening for Thermodiffusively Unstable Lean Hydrogen Flames in Homogeneous Isotropic Turbulence

title: Development and assessment of a target-$ω$ interfacial turbulence-damping model for stratified gas--liquid flow
authors: Di Wu, Junda Liu, Qiaopeng Wang, Liu Liu, Dongling Wu, Ping Zhou
abstract: Interfacial turbulence damping is required in Reynolds-averaged simulations of stratified gas--liquid flows when strong interfacial velocity gradients are present. In this work, we develop a target-$ω$ interfacial damping formulation for the low-Reynolds-number Wilcox-type $k$--$ω$ model in a one-field RANS/VOF framework. A gas-side target value of the specific dissipation rate $ω$ is constructed from an effective interfacial wall coordinate determined from the local resolved flow. The constructed target-$ω$ provides a smooth transition between the viscous and logarithmic limits through power-law blending and requires no calibration of model constants against target data. \textcolor{black}{The formulation is first assessed against three gas-layer DNS cases at $Re_τ\simeq180$ with different interface velocities. The model reproduces the principal features of the mean velocity, turbulent kinetic energy and Reynolds shear-stress distributions, while showing substantially weaker sensitivity to the near-interface grid resolution than the Egorov-type formulation, although some grid dependence remains on the coarsest mesh. The assessment is then extended to the co-current Fabre stratified-flow experiment at a higher Reynolds number and to the counter-current Stäbler experiment}. In both cases, the present formulation provides generally good predictions of the gas-side mean flow and turbulence statistics without case-specific adjustment. For the Stäbler case, in which the liquid level develops as part of the coupled two-phase solution, the predicted mean liquid depth agrees closely with the measured value. These results indicate that the target-$ω$ formulation provides a consistent interfacial turbulence-damping treatment for resolved large gas--liquid interfaces over the range of conditions considered.

infographic.key_insight: A target-ω model damps interfacial turbulence in stratified gas–liquid flow without calibration against target data, while reducing near-interface grid sensitivity relative to an Egorov-type formulation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The formulation supports RANS predictions of gas-side flow and turbulence in stratified two-phase systems, including coupled liquid-depth prediction.
method: Embed interfacial damping in a low-Reynolds-number Wilcox-type k–ω model within a one-field RANS/VOF framework.
Construct a gas-side target ω from an effective interfacial wall coordinate based on the local resolved flow.
Use power-law blending for a smooth transition between viscous and logarithmic limits.
infographic.evidence_signal: Assessment against three gas-layer DNS cases at Reτ ≈ 180 and the Fabre co-current and Stäbler counter-current experiments showed generally good gas-side predictions and close agreement with measured liquid depth in the Stäbler case.
infographic.watch_item: Some grid dependence remains on the coarsest mesh, and validation is limited to the resolved-interface conditions studied.
infographic.paper_title: Development and assessment of a target-$ω$ interfacial turbulence-damping model for stratified gas--liquid flow

title: State-augmented deep reinforcement learning for active flow control around an elliptical cylinder
authors: Wang Jia, Hang Xu
abstract: We employ reinforcement learning algorithms to develop control strategies for manipulating synthetic jets on an elliptical cylinder, targeting robust flow control across varying aspect ratios (Ar). Our results show that for high aspect ratios (Ar = 1 and 0.75), the learned strategies effectively mitigate vortex shedding, achieving drag reductions of 13.4% and 20.1%, respectively. As the Ar decreases, more complex wake dynamics challenge flow control. For Ar = 0.5 and 0.25, drag reductions of 26.88% and 30.37% are achieved, though vortex suppression becomes increasingly difficult. For extremely slender cylinders (Ar = 0.1), we enhance control performance by enriching dynamic feature representation and using Kalman filtering for state estimation. Unlike conventional methods, our approach successfully achieves complete vortex shedding suppression, a maximum drag reduction of 32.2%, and eliminates periodic oscillations, stabilizing the flow. These results demonstrate the efficacy of state-enhanced RL in controlling highly slender geometries.

infographic.key_insight: State-augmented reinforcement learning controls synthetic jets around elliptical cylinders, achieving complete vortex-shedding suppression and up to 32.2% drag reduction at aspect ratio 0.1.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could enable active drag reduction and wake stabilization around slender structures with challenging flow dynamics.
method: Learn synthetic-jet actuation strategies using deep reinforcement learning.
Evaluate control across elliptical-cylinder aspect ratios from 1 to 0.1.
Enrich dynamic state features and apply Kalman filtering for the most slender geometry.
infographic.evidence_signal: Reported drag reductions are 13.4%, 20.1%, 26.88%, and 30.37% at aspect ratios 1, 0.75, 0.5, and 0.25, respectively, with a maximum of 32.2% at 0.1.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not report actuator energy costs or experimental validation, leaving net efficiency and real-world robustness uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: State-augmented deep reinforcement learning for active flow control around an elliptical cylinder

title: Solving and Learning Navier-Stokes Dynamics with the Neural Basis Method
authors: Yuhe Wang, Zhu Wang, Min Wang
abstract: Physics-informed machine learning has become a major direction in predictive modeling of fluid dynamics, combining governing physics with learned representations. Yet prevailing formulations neither guarantee that small PDE-residual losses imply small solution errors nor scale effectively with increasing problem size. Here we present the neural basis method (NBM) as a new approach for Navier--Stokes dynamics. NBM is built on a ``representation-then-projection'' principle: fixed neural bases define the representation space, while projection of the governing equations determines the expansion coefficients. The same bases define common coordinates for the parametric solution manifold, recasting operator learning as a parameter-to-coefficient mapping and enabling scalability by removing explicit spatial dependence. For incompressible flow, NBM yields a velocity-only formulation whose residual provides an a posteriori velocity-error estimate, establishing a certified, data-free training objective for coefficient learning. Theoretical analysis and numerical experiments demonstrate the accuracy, efficiency, generalization, and scalability of NBM, with substantial improvements over baselines.

infographic.key_insight: The neural basis method separates fixed neural representations from physics-based projection to solve and learn Navier–Stokes dynamics in shared coefficient coordinates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Learning parameter-to-coefficient maps rather than spatially dependent solution maps offers a scalable route to predictive fluid modeling.
method: Represent flow solutions using fixed neural basis functions.
Project governing equations to determine expansion coefficients.
Learn parameter-to-coefficient maps using a velocity-only residual with an a posteriori velocity-error estimate.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical analysis and numerical experiments showing improvements over baselines in accuracy, efficiency, generalization, and scalability, without specifying benchmarks or quantitative gains.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy depends on how well the fixed basis represents the target flows; robustness beyond the evaluated parameter regimes remains to be assessed.
infographic.paper_title: Solving and Learning Navier-Stokes Dynamics with the Neural Basis Method

title: Quantum hydrodynamics from Nambu's unpublished fluid notes
authors: Kazuki Ikeda
abstract: We develop a quantum hydrodynamic theory based on Nambu's unpublished note \emph{A New Look at Fluid Dynamics}. The kinetic action defines a metric on configuration space and a mechanical connection coupling an observable cyclic deformation to unobserved fluid modes. Tracing out these modes yields a quantum channel for the observed deformation. We establish a criterion for the exact preservation of coherence between opposite momenta and show how nonzero connection curvature prevents this coupling from being removed. The leading quadratic decay of quantum coherence is determined by the prepared quantum state. For two shear flows, we identify an exact noiseless sign subsystem. Introducing additional generating flows cancels the initial residual of the Euler equations while producing nonzero connection curvature, governed by the same kinetic integrals that determine the classical correction. At fixed mean energy, choosing amplitudes adapted to the dominant coupling flow substantially reduces the initial decoherence, even along the direction that cancels the Euler residual. This advantage gradually diminishes under conditional evolution, eventually leading to a crossing of the decoherence curves. Our example shows that a preparation with a smaller initial coherence-decay coefficient can have a larger maximum sampled loss over a finite readout interval.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum coherence in an observed fluid deformation depends on its coupling to hidden modes and their prepared state, with nonzero connection curvature preventing that coupling from being removed.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework suggests ways to preserve coherence in quantum fluid models through mode selection and state preparation, while accounting for finite-time performance.
method: Derive a configuration-space metric and mechanical connection from the fluid kinetic action.
Trace out unobserved modes to obtain a quantum channel and criteria for coherence preservation.
Analyze shear flows and added generating flows to connect Euler-residual cancellation, curvature, and decoherence.
infographic.evidence_signal: Analytical flow examples identify an exact noiseless sign subsystem and show that energy-matched preparations with lower initial decoherence can later exhibit greater maximum sampled coherence loss.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports theoretical examples rather than experimental validation, and optimizing initial coherence decay does not guarantee better finite-time performance.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum hydrodynamics from Nambu's unpublished fluid notes

title: Physics-Constrained Symbolic Regression for Mean-Velocity and Mixing-Length Scaling in Zero-Pressure-Gradient Turbulent Boundary Layers
authors: Xianglin Shan, Weiwei Zhang
abstract: Developing interpretable full-profile relations for mean velocity and effective mixing length remains challenging because the near-wall, overlap, and outer regions exhibit distinct scaling behaviors. In this paper, physics-constrained symbolic regression is used to construct analytical relations for incompressible zero-pressure-gradient turbulent boundary layers. Classical logarithmic and Prandtl mixing-length scalings provide the starting points, while the regression identifies near-wall transition functions under asymptotic constraints and Reynolds-number-dependent outer corrections. The resulting expressions retain the prescribed leading-order near-wall exponents, reproduce the principal overlap-region behavior, and describe finite-Reynolds-number variations. The mean-velocity relation agrees well with 35 profiles from direct numerical simulations, large-eddy simulations, and experiments spanning friction Reynolds numbers from 252 to 72,526, while the mixing-length relation captures the principal trends in the simulation-derived data. These results illustrate how physical scaling knowledge can guide symbolic regression toward compact, interpretable analytical descriptions of canonical wall turbulence.

infographic.key_insight: Physics-constrained symbolic regression yields compact, interpretable relations for mean velocity and effective mixing length across zero-pressure-gradient turbulent boundary layers.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These analytical relations can support engineering calculations requiring full-profile velocity and mixing-length descriptions across Reynolds numbers.
method: Start from logarithmic velocity and Prandtl mixing-length scalings.
Identify near-wall transition functions while enforcing asymptotic constraints.
Introduce Reynolds-number-dependent outer corrections.
infographic.evidence_signal: The mean-velocity relation agrees well with 35 DNS, LES, and experimental profiles spanning friction Reynolds numbers of 252–72,526; the mixing-length relation captures principal trends in simulation-derived data.
infographic.watch_item: Applicability beyond incompressible zero-pressure-gradient boundary layers is not established by the reported evaluation.
infographic.paper_title: Physics-Constrained Symbolic Regression for Mean-Velocity and Mixing-Length Scaling in Zero-Pressure-Gradient Turbulent Boundary Layers

title: A Graph-informed Kriging model for sample-efficient Bayesian optimization of wind farm layouts
authors: Zhen-Fan Wang, Kai Zhang, Xianping Du, Zhaolong Han, Dai Zhou, Onur Bilgen
abstract: Wind farm layout optimization becomes increasingly difficult as turbine count grows, especially when high-fidelity aerodynamic models are used. Conventional Kriging-based Bayesian optimization often suffers from low sample efficiency in high-dimensional layout spaces because sparse training data provide limited domain coverage. We develop a Graph-informed Kriging framework that embeds reusable aerodynamic interaction information into the surrogate mean function. The wind farm is represented as a directed aerodynamic graph, where pairwise turbine interactions defined in a low-dimensional relative-coordinate space are assembled into a farm-scale mean. This structured mean captures the dominant variation in annual energy production (AEP), allowing the Gaussian process to model only the residual structure and uncertainty. Numerical experiments show that Graph-informed Kriging consistently improves AEP prediction accuracy over ordinary and generic-trend Kriging under sparse-data conditions, with increasing benefits as layout dimension and wake-interaction strength grow. Embedded in Bayesian optimization, it substantially improves sample efficiency and achieves competitive solutions for the IEA Wind Task 37 benchmark with about 280 AEP evaluations. In a controlled 16-turbine case, it also outperforms ordinary and multi-fidelity Kriging under the same high-fidelity evaluation budget. The framework is further extended to a 48-turbine wind farm, demonstrating applicability to large-scale CFD-based layout optimization. These results show that Graph-informed surrogate modeling can enable more efficient use of high-fidelity aerodynamic models for reliable large-scale wind farm layout design.

infographic.key_insight: Embedding graph-based turbine interactions into a Kriging surrogate improves sample-efficient Bayesian optimization of wind farm layouts.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach can reduce costly aerodynamic evaluations needed to design high-energy-yield wind farms, including large-scale CFD-based layouts.
method: Represent turbines and directed aerodynamic interactions as a graph.
Assemble low-dimensional pairwise interaction models into a farm-scale mean for annual energy production.
Use a Gaussian process to model residual structure and uncertainty within Bayesian optimization.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports competitive IEA Wind Task 37 solutions with about 280 AEP evaluations, better performance than ordinary and multi-fidelity Kriging in a controlled 16-turbine case, and extension to 48 turbines.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may depend on how well reusable pairwise interactions capture the aerodynamics of new layouts and operating conditions.
infographic.paper_title: A Graph-informed Kriging model for sample-efficient Bayesian optimization of wind farm layouts

title: Automated Discovery of Physically Interpretable Subgrid Length Scales for Detached Eddy Simulation via Agentic AI
authors: Jiawei Chen, Xiang I. A. Yang, Ping He
abstract: Traditional turbulence-model development relies heavily on expert knowledge and is time-consuming. This study develops an agentic AI framework, DEScover (automated Discovery of DES closures), to explore subgrid length scales for detached eddy simulation (DES). The user provides only a modeling idea: the length scale is the grid width normal to the local vortex axis. Four large language model (LLM) agents then propose, review, implement, and evaluate candidate formulations and generate scripts for CFD simulations. The Discovery Agent infers the vortex axis from various vortex-identification methods. The candidates are tested on four cases spanning canonical and engineering flows: a flat plate, a backward-facing step, a free shear layer, and an iced airfoil. For all test cases, the best candidate consistently outperforms the standard length scale based on the maximum cell size. Its accuracy is similar to, or slightly better than, that of the expert-designed shear-layer-adapted length scale. Each agentic discovery run takes about 25 minutes on average, excluding the CFD simulations. These results show that LLM-based reasoning can significantly accelerate the discovery of physically interpretable turbulence models and reduce reliance on manual expert formulation.

infographic.key_insight: DEScover uses four LLM agents to discover physically interpretable DES subgrid length scales based on grid width normal to the local vortex axis.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could accelerate turbulence-model development while improving DES accuracy over the standard maximum-cell-size length scale.
method: Start from a user-supplied physical modeling idea.
Use four agents to propose, review, implement, and evaluate candidate formulations.
Infer vortex axes using vortex-identification methods and generate CFD simulation scripts.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across a flat plate, backward-facing step, free shear layer, and iced airfoil, the best candidate outperformed the standard length scale and matched or slightly exceeded an expert-designed shear-layer-adapted scale.
infographic.watch_item: The reported average discovery time of about 25 minutes excludes CFD simulations, and broader flow and mesh generalization remains to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Automated Discovery of Physically Interpretable Subgrid Length Scales for Detached Eddy Simulation via Agentic AI

title: Local Metrics for Exact Streaming on Curvilinear Lattices: A Curvilinear D3Q27 Cumulant Lattice-Boltzmann Method
authors: Maher Sawaf, Jonas Latt, Nikolaus A. Adams, Mostafa S. Shadloo
abstract: A three-dimensional curvilinear lattice-Boltzmann method is introduced for simulations on smoothly deformed grids while retaining exact one-to-one streaming on a uniform computational lattice. The coordinate transformation is represented locally through a metric-Gaussian equilibrium and a Christoffel-connection source in moment space. A dynamically reconstructed homogeneous-state perturbation streaming procedure preserves homogeneous physical states on warped meshes without interpolation in the advection step. The method is implemented on a D3Q27 lattice with a cumulant collision operator, while the geometric construction remains compatible with other local collision models. The formulation is assessed using two sets of tests. First, static non-orthogonal warped-cube cases validate the bulk curvilinear solver through a convected helical shear wave, the Taylor--Green vortex, and Arnold--Beltrami--Childress flow. These tests verify viscous decay, clean freestream preservation, vortex-breakdown dynamics, and the nonlinear inertial--pressure balance induced by geometric acceleration. Second, wall-bounded and moving-boundary demonstrations assess the boundary-compatible extension through warped plane Poiseuille flow, arbitrary Lagrangian--Eulerian (ALE) peristaltic pumping, and a two-way fluid--structure interaction (FSI) case with added-mass frequency shift. The results show that the proposed curvilinear LBM avoids interpolation-based transport, reduces geometry-locked numerical modes, preserves global mass and momentum to round-off accuracy in the tested warped periodic cases, and extends to wall-bounded ALE/FSI configurations with conservative treatment of mass and physically consistent momentum exchange.

infographic.key_insight: A curvilinear D3Q27 cumulant lattice-Boltzmann method retains exact one-to-one streaming on a uniform computational lattice while representing smoothly warped physical grids through local geometry.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports complex-grid flow simulation and moving-boundary fluid–structure interaction without interpolation-based advection.
method: Encode local geometry with a metric-Gaussian equilibrium and a Christoffel-connection source in moment space.
Dynamically reconstruct homogeneous-state perturbations to preserve uniform physical flow on warped meshes.
Use D3Q27 cumulant collision with boundary-compatible ALE and two-way FSI extensions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Warped-grid shear-wave, Taylor–Green, ABC-flow, Poiseuille, peristaltic-pumping, and FSI tests assess flow dynamics and boundary coupling; tested warped periodic cases conserve global mass and momentum to round-off accuracy.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish robustness limits for severe grid deformation or quantify computational overhead.
infographic.paper_title: Local Metrics for Exact Streaming on Curvilinear Lattices: A Curvilinear D3Q27 Cumulant Lattice-Boltzmann Method

title: Rotation-driven suppression and re-emergence of unsteady flow past a circular cylinder
authors: Aditi Sengupta, Sanjeev Kumar, Puneet Kumar
abstract: The flow past a rotating cylinder undergoes substantial changes in its wake dynamics and aerodynamic response with increasing rotation rate. This study investigates these changes in two-dimensional compressible flow at \(Re_\infty=3800\) and \(M_\infty=0.1\), with the rotation rate systematically varied over \(0.1\leqΩ\leq10\) using 130 high-fidelity simulations. At low rotation rates, conventional periodic vortex shedding is progressively suppressed with increasing rotation. A narrow transition regime around \(Ω=2.2-2.8\) is identified, where sustained oscillations evolve into intermittent fluctuations before reaching a nearly quiescent state. At higher rotation rates, unsteadiness re-emerges with distinctly intermittent and multiscale characteristics, demonstrating that this instability is fundamentally different from conventional Kármán shedding. The surface pressure and streamwise skin-friction distributions reveal substantial redistribution of aerodynamic loading with rotation, characterized by increasingly intense suction and significant modification of the near-wall shear field. The maximum lift increases systematically with rotation, reflecting the strengthening Magnus-Robins effect, whereas drag exhibits a non-monotonic response with enhanced variability at high rotation rates. Despite the low free-stream Mach number, rotational acceleration produces local Mach numbers approaching 0.5, indicating appreciable compressibility effects in the near-cylinder region. Vorticity-based proper orthogonal decomposition further reveals a transition from wake-dominated coherent structures at low rotation to strongly wrapped, rotation-dominated structures at high rotation. These results establish a direct connection between rotational forcing, surface loading, compressibility, and the suppression and subsequent re-emergence of flow unsteadiness.

infographic.key_insight: Increasing cylinder rotation suppresses conventional vortex shedding before unsteadiness re-emerges at high rotation as intermittent, multiscale flow.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Rotation offers a means to control wake dynamics and lift, but non-monotonic drag and renewed unsteadiness complicate operating-point selection.
method: 130 high-fidelity, two-dimensional compressible-flow simulations at Re∞ = 3800 and M∞ = 0.1.
Rotation-rate sweep over 0.1 ≤ Ω ≤ 10 with surface-pressure, skin-friction, and aerodynamic-force analysis.
Vorticity-based proper orthogonal decomposition to characterize coherent flow structures.
infographic.evidence_signal: The simulations identify a suppression transition around Ω = 2.2–2.8, followed at higher rotation by renewed intermittency and local Mach numbers approaching 0.5.
infographic.watch_item: The two-dimensional setup and fixed Reynolds and free-stream Mach numbers limit direct extrapolation to three-dimensional engineering flows.
infographic.paper_title: Rotation-driven suppression and re-emergence of unsteady flow past a circular cylinder

title: Learning the solution operator of standing waves with a Fourier neural operator
authors: Changhong Mou, Savana Ammons, Di Qi, Vera Mikyoung Hur
abstract: The standing wave problem concerns the space-time periodic motion at the free surface of a two-dimensional, infinitely deep, irrotational flow of an incompressible inviscid fluid under gravity. Although spectrally accurate computations have revealed a rich array of nonlinear wave phenomena, repeatedly evaluating their evolution over large parameter spaces remains challenging, particularly when resolving fine-scale spatial oscillations. We employ a Fourier neural operator (FNO) architecture to learn the solution operator along a numerically computed one-parameter family of symmetric standing waves. Given a wave profile at an instant of rest and a normalized observation time, the learned operator predicts the fluid surface, the velocity potential and the dipole density at the surface at that time. In-distribution tests yield uniformly small relative errors within the training range. Two out-of-distribution experiments characterize extrapolation toward contrasting physical regimes. Toward the free-fall limit, errors concentrate near the sharpening crest, consistent with the spectral truncation in the FNO architecture. Toward the linear limit, absolute errors remain small whereas relative errors increase as the amplitude vanishes. A residual of the governing equations, evaluated independently of reference solutions, complements these tests and provides a diagnostic for exploratory predictions beyond the available data.

infographic.key_insight: A Fourier neural operator learns a numerically computed family of nonlinear standing waves, predicting free-surface geometry, velocity potential and surface dipole density.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The surrogate offers a route to efficient repeated evaluation of idealized free-surface waves across a parameterized family.
method: Train on a one-parameter family of symmetric standing waves in infinitely deep, inviscid, irrotational flow.
Map an initial wave profile at rest and normalized observation time to three surface fields.
Evaluate extrapolation toward free-fall and linear limits, alongside an independent governing-equation residual.
infographic.evidence_signal: In-distribution tests show uniformly small relative errors; extrapolation errors localize near sharpening crests toward free fall, while relative errors grow as amplitudes vanish toward the linear limit.
infographic.watch_item: Validation is limited to one standing-wave family, and FNO spectral truncation can hinder resolution of sharp crests.
infographic.paper_title: Learning the solution operator of standing waves with a Fourier neural operator

title: Flow Mesh: A Velocity-Regularized Flow Matching Framework for Stable Distributional Modeling of Physical Fields on Unstructured Meshes
authors: Siddharth Verma, Jaewan Park, Jay Phil Yoo, Kazuma Kobayashi, Souvik Chakraborty, Syed Bahauddin Alam
abstract: Thermal-fluid field distributions underpin the analysis and operation of energy infrastructure, from nuclear-reactor cooling channels to industrial heat exchangers, but resolving these distributions through computational fluid dynamics requires prohibitively large simulation ensembles. Their complex geometries also demand unstructured meshes that are poorly accommodated by generative models developed for regular grids. Here we introduce FlowMesh, a generative framework that combines permutation-invariant mesh encoding with deterministic latent flow matching and an l1 penalty on the learned transport velocity. FlowMesh generates full-field realizations directly on fixed unstructured meshes without auxiliary grid interpolation or a stochastic denoising chain. Across lid-driven-cavity, pressurized-water-reactor subchannel and heat-exchanger datasets, evaluated over six matched training seeds, FlowMesh achieves macro-averaged probability-density-function coverage of 91.7%-97.0%, exceeding an architecture-controlled latent diffusion model by $11.6$--$45.4$ percentage points. Latent-velocity regularization increases coverage by $3.8$ percentage points for reactor flows and 1.1 points for heat-exchanger flows, while reducing temperature-field Kullback--Leibler divergence by 1.7-2.4-fold. Each full-field realization requires 1.23 \pm 0.15 s, providing a 585--1902-fold wall-clock acceleration over computational fluid dynamics. FlowMesh therefore makes large-scale generative characterization of thermal-fluid states computationally feasible, providing a foundation for data-driven analysis and digital-twin development in fixed-geometry energy systems.

infographic.key_insight: FlowMesh generates thermal-fluid fields directly on unstructured meshes, improving distributional coverage over latent diffusion while accelerating sampling relative to CFD.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Fast full-field sampling could enable large-ensemble thermal-fluid analysis and digital twins for fixed-geometry reactor cooling channels and heat exchangers.
method: Permutation-invariant encoding of unstructured meshes.
Deterministic latent flow matching without grid interpolation or stochastic denoising.
L1 regularization of learned transport velocity.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three datasets and six matched training seeds, FlowMesh achieved 91.7–97.0% macro-averaged PDF coverage, exceeding architecture-controlled latent diffusion by 11.6–45.4 percentage points, with 585–1902× wall-clock speedups over CFD.
infographic.watch_item: Results concern fixed meshes and geometries; generalization to unseen geometries or operating regimes is not established by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Flow Mesh: A Velocity-Regularized Flow Matching Framework for Stable Distributional Modeling of Physical Fields on Unstructured Meshes

title: DSMC Study on Unsteadiness of Supersonic Flow Over a Cylinder
authors: Mert Senkardesler, Irmak T. Karpuzcu, Deborah A. Levin
abstract: Unsteady flow over a 30 $μ$m diameter cylinder at Mach 4 is investigated using Direct Simulation Monte Carlo across Reynolds numbers from 270 to 6750, spanning slip-flow to near-continuum regimes. Power Spectral Density analysis at discrete probe locations and Dynamic Mode Decomposition of flowfield snapshots independently characterize instabilities in both the stagnation and wake regions. In the stagnation region, a bow shock pulsation mode at 10-15 MHz frequency is identified across all cases despite a 24-fold variation in number density. In the wake, two distinct instabilities are observed. The canonical vortex shedding mode at Strouhal number St $\approx$ 0.2 dominates at lower Reynolds numbers. A second instability at St $\approx$ 0.5, consistent with previously reported slipline-driven oscillations in supersonic wakes, emerges at higher Reynolds numbers and progressively strengthens, becoming the dominant mode. In the studied Reynolds range, the wake transitions from no clear unsteadiness, to canonical vortex shedding at St $\approx$ 0.20, and reaching a regime where the St $\approx$ 0.5 mode becomes dominant, while also having a distinct independent bow shock pulsation possibly governed by its standoff distance.

infographic.key_insight: Mach 4 flow over a microscale cylinder exhibits a wake transition from no clear unsteadiness to vortex shedding at St ≈ 0.2 and then dominance of a second mode at St ≈ 0.5, alongside independent bow-shock pulsations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These instability regimes can inform unsteady-load and flow-control assessments for microscale bodies in supersonic, rarefied-to-near-continuum flows.
method: Direct Simulation Monte Carlo for a 30 μm cylinder at Mach 4 and Re = 270–6750.
Power spectral density analysis at discrete flow probes.
Dynamic mode decomposition of flowfield snapshots.
infographic.evidence_signal: Both analyses identify stagnation- and wake-region instabilities, with 10–15 MHz bow-shock pulsations present across all cases despite a 24-fold number-density variation.
infographic.watch_item: Bow-shock standoff distance is only a proposed control mechanism for pulsation, and the abstract does not establish broader applicability beyond the studied conditions.
infographic.paper_title: DSMC Study on Unsteadiness of Supersonic Flow Over a Cylinder

title: High-Fidelity Aerostructural Dataset of Transonic Wings in Cruise Conditions
authors: Pavankumar Koratikere, Abhijnan Dikshit, Leifur Leifsson
abstract: Recent advances in machine learning (ML) have the potential to substantially accelerate aircraft wing design, a process that has traditionally required extensive high-fidelity simulation and design iteration. Existing public datasets for ML-based wing design have focused primarily on aerodynamic performance, with limited consideration of the multidisciplinary interactions that govern practical aircraft design. In particular, efficient wing design requires simultaneous consideration of aerodynamic performance and structural integrity, yet no publicly available datasets capture this coupled aerostructural behavior at high-fidelity. To address this need, a high-fidelity multidisciplinary dataset for static aerostructural analysis of transonic wings is introduced. The dataset includes 2471 samples, along with three out-of-distribution samples. The wing planform geometry is parameterized by span, sweep, dihedral, tip chord, and tip twist, while the airfoil cross-sections are parameterized using the class-shape transformation method. The analysis is further parameterized by Mach number, angle of attack, altitude, and structural load factor. The utility of the dataset is demonstrated by training state-of-the-art ML models to predict aerodynamic surface quantities, integrated aerodynamic performance quantities, and the failure distribution of the wingbox. ML models achieve at most 0.0309 normalized root mean squared error (NRMSE) in the prediction of aerodynamic quantities and at most 0.1189 NRMSE in the prediction of failure distribution of the wingbox. By providing coupled aerodynamic and structural responses for a diverse set of transonic wings, this dataset establishes a benchmark for developing, evaluating, and comparing multi-physics ML models for wing design. Broadly, it is intended to encourage creation of similar high-fidelity multi-physics benchmark datasets across engineering domains.

infographic.key_insight: A high-fidelity transonic-wing dataset couples aerodynamic and structural responses to benchmark machine learning for multidisciplinary wing design.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The dataset supports ML surrogates that could accelerate wing design while accounting for both aerodynamic performance and structural integrity.
method: Parameterize wing planforms and airfoil sections using geometric variables and class-shape transformation.
Perform static aerostructural analyses across Mach number, angle of attack, altitude, and structural load factor.
Train ML models to predict aerodynamic surface quantities, integrated performance, and wingbox failure distributions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The dataset contains 2,471 samples plus 3 out-of-distribution samples; reported ML NRMSE is at most 0.0309 for aerodynamic quantities and 0.1189 for wingbox failure distributions.
infographic.watch_item: Only three out-of-distribution samples are included, limiting evidence of generalization beyond the sampled design and operating conditions.
infographic.paper_title: High-Fidelity Aerostructural Dataset of Transonic Wings in Cruise Conditions
